response.answer: To simulate power for mixed models, use `simr` with `makeLmer` for linear mixed models. Specify fixed and random effects, then run `power_lmer` in `simr`. For random slopes, include `(1|group) + (1|group:predictor)`.

results.title: Chapter 14 Beyond Superpower I: Mixed Models with simr | Power Analysis with Superpower
results.content: # Chapter 14 Beyond Superpower I: Mixed Models with `simr`. One of the most common situations is the introduction of “random” effects (i.e., mixed models), or the distribution of the dependent variable may not be “normal” (e.g., it may be a binary, 0 or 1, response). This is a flexible power analysis tool that can be used for linear mixed models *and* for generalized linear mixed models. Essentially, it builds a model using the `makeLmer` or `makeGlmer` functions and then simulates data (using `lme4` under-the-hood) to estimate the power of the model given the specified parameters. For example, from the `simr` vignettes, we can imagine a study where a researcher has three levels for a random effect. We then have a variable, “x,” and we want to see our power to detect this effect on outcome “y.” The data we need for `simr` could be generated with the following code. library(simr) library # Some covariate that we have measured at 10 different levels # Some covariate that we have measured at 10 different levelsx <- rep(1:10)<- rep 1: 10 # Three random grouping variables # Three random grouping variables # (e.g., Petri dishes)# (e.g., Petri dishes)g <- c('a', 'b', 'c')<- c 'a' 'b' 'c' # Comine into 1 dataset # Comine into 1 datasetX <- expand.grid(x=x, g=g)<-expand.gridx=g=. Now we can define our model a little bit further by assigned the fixed and random effects. For this model we need to provide 2 slope coefficients, and the random intercept variance. We then need to build a mixed model using the `makeLmer` function. In this case we define a new outcome variable (`y`) then assign a fixed effect for `x`, and provide the random effect structure as random intercept only (`(1|g)`). ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: y ~ x + (1 | g) ## Data: X ## REML criterion at convergence: 93.2416 ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Std.Dev. Please note that the total number of observations and data structure (3 levels for the random effect) will be the same in these simulations. “SIMR : An r Package for Power Analysis of Generalized Linear Mixed Models by Simulation.” Edited by Shinichi Nakagawa.

results.content: The r package simr allows users to calculate power for generalized linear mixed models from the lme4 package. ## The simr package There are a range of r packages (see Fig. 1) currently available for power analysis of mixed models (Martin *et al*. ### Running the Power Analysis Once the model and effect size have been specified, a power analysis is very easy in simr. * model2 <- extend(model1, along="x", n=20) * ## Power for predictor 'x', (95% confidence interval): * ## 96.60% (95.28, 97.63) * ## Effect size for x is -0.05 * ## Based on 1000 simulations, (28 warnings, 0 errors) * ## alpha = 0.05, nrow = 60 * ## Time elapsed: 0 h 3 m 37 s The along argument specifies which variable is being extended, and n specifies how many levels to replace it with. We can extend this to five observations per site per year as follows: * model4 <- extend(model1, within="x+g", n=5) * pc4 <- powerCurve(model4, within="x+g", breaks=1:5) * ## Power for predictor 'x', (95% confidence interval), * ## by number of observations within x+g: * ## 1: 33.90% (30.97, 36.93) - 30 rows * ## 2: 58.00% (54.87, 61.08) - 60 rows * ## 3: 74.40% (71.58, 77.08) - 90 rows * ## 4: 86.30% (84.01, 88.37) - 120 rows * ## 5: 91.80% (89.92, 93.43) - 150 rows * ## Time elapsed: 0 h 11 m 35 s Note the breaks argument to powerCurve. ## Further work Version 1.0 of simr is designed for any LMM or GLMM fitted using lmer or glmer in the lme4 package, and for any linear or generalized linear model using lm or glm, and is focussed on calculating power for hypothesis tests. 10.1111/j.1442-9993.2007.01715.x Web of Science® Google Scholar (2013) Linear Mixed-Effects Models Using R: A Step-by-Step Approach. 10.1016/j.jenvman.2005.04.016 PubMed Web of Science® Google Scholar (2012) pamm: power analysis for random effects in mixed models. 10.1111/j.1600-0587.2011.06370.x Web of Science® Google Scholar (2008) Size and power of tests for a zero random effect variance or polynomial regression in additive and linear mixed models.

results.title: r - Calculating minimum sample size required for repeated measures linear mixed model using the simr package - Cross Validated
results.content: # Calculating minimum sample size required for repeated measures linear mixed model using the simr package. I would like to use the `simr` package to calculate the smallest sample size needed to achieve $0.80$ power at the $0.05$ alpha level while accounting for a small effect size. The `simr` package appears to calculate simulations based on an alpha level of $0.05$, a power level of $0.80$, and a small effect size, but I do not see how I would account for the repeated measures aspect of the study. It is quite flexible in that you can specify your simulated power analysis by raw data that you have on hand or some a priori specification of what you expect the effects to be. The example they give is a crossed effects mixed model, which multiplies the subject by item observations. If we inspect our model with `summary(artificial_glmer)`, we should see the same fixed and random effects we asked for:. We input our previously specified model and data, note that we want the fixed effects of native language and frequency, we ask for the subject estimates (for how many subjects we need in this design), how many subjects we want to estimate (from $20$ subjects to $180$, the critical value we need to surpass ($2$ here is a simplification for the $1.96$ cutoff in NHST tests), the number of simulations (should be large like $100$ or $1,000$ but here I use $10$ to make it faster), and the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI), which is explained in the article). #### Run Mixedpower Sim #### power <- mixedpower(model = artificial_glmer, data = artificial_data, fixed_effects = c("NativeLanguage", "CenteredFrequency"), simvar = "Subject", steps = c(20,60,100,140,180), critical_value = 2, n_sim = 100, SESOI = c(-4.3, 0.30 ,-0.34, -0.27)). PowerSim function (simr package) indicates 100% power for small sample dataset, regardless of effect size, alpha level, or if fixed/random slopes. 1") How to calculate sample size for linear regression when you know the power, effect size, no. 1") How to determine sample size needed for sufficient power to compare between levels of a fixed effect in a mixed model? 3") What would "small", "medium," and "large" effect sizes be for mixed effects model in simr?

results.title: r - Using a variable as a fixed effect and random effects grouping variable in linear mixed effects model - Cross Validated
results.content: # Using a variable as a fixed effect and random effects grouping variable in linear mixed effects model. I've read quite a few of the other posts regarding linear mixed effects models and have come across papers like the Barr et al., 2013 paper suggesting to use the maximal random effects structure for confirmatory hypothesis testing. Since my two factors of interest are the shoe and time of day I have been treating those as fixed effects. However, the shoes and time of day might have a different effect on each subject, so I have been thinking I should include a random slope for these terms as well. **My core question is**: Can I have a random effects structure like the latter? Where I have a fixed effect also used as part of a grouping variable in a random effect? It seems weird to me to look at variation across days as a random effect when part of the variation across days is what I am interested in capturing as part of the "Shoes" fixed effect. Given my design, are there any suggestions on how to decide between the two random effects structures that I am considering? Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. An introduction to linear mixed-effects modeling in R. Best practice guidance for linear mixed-effects models in psychological science. However, I am still concerned whether including a random intercept for the combination of shoe/subject is misinformed if I also have a Shoe fixed effect $\endgroup$. Its acceptable to have as a fixed effect and random slope. Random Slope Linear Mixed Effects Model with Nested Data. results.content: # Constructing the random effects model matrix Z. ## post by Jack\_Caster on Apr 8, 2018. I am trying to replicate the sleep deprivation study found in the R package LME4 (for fitting linear mixed effects models) and described in this paper. > the average reaction time per day for subjects in a sleep deprivation study. What I want to to is to fit a random effects model on intercept and slope for each subject. That is, `X` is the design matrix for the fixed effects given by the formula `Reaction ~ 1 + Days`, and `Z` is the design matrix for the random effects. However, I have some doubts on how to design such matrix `Z` to get intercept’s and slope’s coefficients. What I did is to simply create a design matrix from the formula `Reaction ~ 0 + Subject + Subject:Days`. ## post by junpenglao on Apr 8, 2018. Sometimes (e.g. in `brms` which based on Stan), ppl use an indexing method for the random effects. Khatri-Rao with Kronecker product is more for when you have a random intercept *and* slope model, but you can construct by hand similarly - the aim is to create a sparse matrix Z where there are blocks of values on the diagonal. ~~In case you have not seen it, I have this repository doing mixed effect model with varies libraries and parameterization: ~~ [EDIT] Just realized I already reply to you about this repo on a similar topic before. ## post by Jack\_Caster on Apr 9, 2018. As I want to have a random effect on intercept **and** slope, either I construct the matrix `Z` as `Reaction ~ 0 + Subject + Subject:Days` (as I did), or I construct the same matrix with the fancy Khatri-Rao method. No problem But it seems you do not have an example with random effects on slopes, or do you? ## post by junpenglao on Apr 9, 2018. What you are doing in your notebook is correct. Also, I agree with your approach separating the random intercept and slope instead of multiplying a big matrix - you have much more controls on the prior. ## post by Jack\_Caster on Apr 9, 2018.
